question: Does fitting a top-k sparse autoencoder to the final encoder residual stream of an RL-trained 100-node neural TSP solver reveal stable, human-interpretable geometric computations, and does the paper quantitatively or causally connect those features to routing performance?

key_findings.claim: The paper transfers a top-k sparse-autoencoder pipeline to the final encoder residual stream of a neural TSP policy and chooses one configuration from a 24-point grid using qualitative interpretability plus reconstruction error.
key_findings.evidence: The authors train an RL4CO graph-Transformer/pointer-style policy on uniformly sampled 100-node unit-square instances, collect final-residual activations from 100,000 same-distribution inference instances, and sweep expansion factor {1,4,16}, k-ratio {0.01,0.10}, and L1 coefficient {0.0001,0.001,0.01,0.1}. They select expansion factor 4, k-ratio 0.1, and L1 coefficient 0.001; neither per-configuration scores nor a reproducible selection rule are reported.

anchors.section: 4.2–4.3 Sparse Autoencoder and Training the SAE

key_findings.claim: The result evidence is a small qualitative gallery of recurring geometric activation patterns, not a quantitative feature inventory.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5 describes feature directions resembling boundary responses, localized focus, and linear separators. Appendix Figure 4 displays 12 overlaid feature examples in four headings—'Activates on the edge,' 'Focuses on one spot,' 'Linearly separated,' and 'Unclear'—using ten TSP instances per visualization. The paper gives no frequency, uncertainty, scorer agreement, held-out selection protocol, or denominator for how many features were inspected.

key_findings.claim: The displayed sparse features establish correlation with input geometry, but do not establish learned TSP heuristics, a decoder circuit, or causal relevance to tour quality.
key_findings.evidence: Activations are summarized and plotted over node coordinates; there is no feature ablation, activation patching, decoder-logit tracing, tour-length intervention, or counterfactual geometry experiment. The authors themselves state that the analysis is correlational and propose connecting residual features to node selection and confirming causality as future work.

key_findings.claim: The PDF does not substantiate its headline claims of approximately 99% optimal routing performance and near-perfect SAE reconstruction with auditable numbers.
key_findings.evidence: The contributions call the policy 'approximately 99% optimal,' say it is benchmarked against Concorde, and later call reconstruction near-perfect. Yet the paper contains no solver-result table, Concorde instance count, optimality-gap definition, mean or distribution, runtime, seed, reconstruction-error value, explained variance, sparsity statistic, or dead-feature rate. The only result figure is the qualitative Appendix A gallery.

key_findings.claim: The neural-solver description is internally ambiguous about whether encoder inputs are static or change during autoregressive decoding.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.1 says each node input includes one-hot indicators for current node, terminal node, and visited status, all of which evolve during tour construction, while the same section says the encoder performs one forward pass for the entire trajectory. Figure 1 instead depicts coordinate input to a static encoder and places current/first-node context plus the visited mask in the decoder. The implementation-resolving detail is not supplied in the paper.

key_findings.claim: The stated top-k equation does not exactly match the prose description of retaining the k largest latent coordinates.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 defines TopK(z)=ReLU(z−tau), with tau the kth-largest activation, while the prose says the k largest activations are retained. The formula shifts every retained value and sends the kth-largest value to zero, so it generally has at most k−1 strictly positive entries rather than preserving k selected coordinates unchanged. Calling this operation differentiable also omits its threshold/tie discontinuities.

key_findings.claim: Qualitative hyperparameter selection on the same distribution used for SAE fitting makes the apparent interpretability vulnerable to selection circularity and instability.
key_findings.evidence: The chosen SAE is selected partly because its features looked interpretable, and the reported visualizations are then used as evidence that interpretable features exist. No held-out feature-scoring protocol, blinded rater, cross-seed match, alternative dictionary method, or out-of-distribution evaluation breaks that loop. The authors explicitly list stability, feature-quality metrics, other distributions and sizes, and non-SAE methods as future work.

key_findings.claim: The paper's sparse-autoencoder reference contains a wrong arXiv identifier, weakening exact source traceability.
key_findings.evidence: Reference [10] labels Gao et al.'s 'Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders' as arXiv:2306.04093. The official arXiv record is arXiv:2406.04093v1; that work is also the direct source for the top-k SAE framework invoked in Sections 4.2–4.3.

method.core_idea: Train a neural construction policy for Euclidean TSP, freeze it, fit an overcomplete sparse dictionary to nodewise final-encoder residual activations, and visually inspect latent directions for recognizable geometric structure.
method.mechanism: A graph Transformer encodes 100 node coordinates and an autoregressive pointer-style decoder selects the tour under a visited-node mask. Training uses a modified clipped REINFORCE objective with a greedy-rollout warmup, sampling temperature, and Adam. A top-k SAE maps final residual vectors to a larger latent dictionary, sparsifies them, reconstructs the residual, and aggregates node activations for coordinate overlays across ten instances.
assumptions: A policy trained only on uniformly sampled 100-node unit-square instances is competitive and representative enough for mechanistic claims about neural TSP solving.
The final encoder residual stream contains a separable dictionary of features rather than distributed or superposed computations that the selected SAE cannot recover.
Low reconstruction error and visually recognizable overlays are meaningful proxies for mechanistic faithfulness.
A mean node-activation summary and ten-instance overlay preserve the information needed to identify feature semantics.
Qualitative model selection and qualitative evaluation by the same researchers do not unduly favor human-recognizable features.
Correlations between latent activations and Euclidean geometry are relevant to decoder decisions and tour length.
The unspecified architecture and dynamic/static input details match the intended RL4CO implementation closely enough to reproduce the analysis.

techniques.role: Provides the frozen encoder-decoder neural TSP solver whose internal residual activations are analyzed.
Optimizes sampled tours with a modified clipped REINFORCE objective after a greedy-rollout warmup.
Collects nodewise representations after the last encoder Transformer block over 100,000 inference instances.
Factorizes residual activations into sparse latent feature directions and reconstructs the original stream.
Sweeps expansion factor, k-ratio, and L1 penalty across 24 configurations before qualitative selection.
Projects mean node activation onto Euclidean TSP plots and overlays ten instances to seek recurring geometry.

evaluations.setting: RL-trained policy on uniformly sampled 100-node Euclidean TSP instances, described in Sections 3–3.2 (pp. 3–4).
evaluations.metric: Purported percentage of Concorde-optimal solution quality.
evaluations.result: The prose reports approximately 99% optimal, but supplies no evaluated instance count, formula, aggregate, dispersion, seed, runtime, or result table.
evaluations.baseline: Concorde is named as the optimal reference, but no Concorde measurements or other neural-solver results appear.

evaluations.setting: Twenty-four SAE configurations trained on final residuals from 100,000 same-distribution N=100 inference instances (pp. 5–6).
evaluations.metric: Qualitative feature interpretability and reconstruction error under expansion factor, k-ratio, and L1 sweeps.
evaluations.result: Expansion factor 4, k-ratio 0.1, and L1 coefficient 0.001 are selected and reconstruction is called near-perfect; no numerical metric, validation split, feature count, or per-grid result is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Other settings in the grid are implicit baselines; PCA, ICA, NMF, standard autoencoders, and other dictionary-learning methods are not evaluated.

evaluations.setting: Feature inspection over ten-instance coordinate overlays, summarized in Section 5 and Appendix A Figure 4 (pp. 6 and 11).
evaluations.metric: Visual resemblance to boundary, local-focus, separating-line, or unclear spatial patterns.
evaluations.result: Twelve displayed panels are grouped under four qualitative labels, including an explicit 'Unclear' group; the total inspected feature population and selection process are unreported.
evaluations.baseline: No random-feature, untrained-policy, alternative-layer, alternative-dictionary, blinded-human, or automated geometry baseline.

evaluations.setting: Causal and external-validity checks proposed in Section 6 (p. 7).
evaluations.metric: Tour/logit change under intervention, stability across seeds, and transfer across N={50,100,200,500} and clustered, ring, or road-like geometries.
evaluations.result: Not conducted in this paper; these tests are explicitly future work.
evaluations.baseline: No causal tracing, cross-seed replication, out-of-distribution instance family, size-transfer, or non-SAE comparison is reported.

limitations: [Author-stated, p. 7 §6] The analysis is correlational; causal tracing from encoder features to decoder node selection and intervention-based confirmation remain future work.
[Author-stated, p. 7 §6] Training and analysis use uniform N=100 instances; transfer to N={50,100,200,500}, clustered Gaussians, rings, and road-like geometry is untested.
[Author-stated, p. 7 §6] Findings may depend on architecture, RL algorithm, reward shaping, learning-rate schedule, exploration noise, and SAE choices.
[Author-stated, p. 7 §6] Cross-seed consistency, reconstruction/sparsity metrics, feature-quality metrics, alternative decomposition methods, and broader neural-CO models are absent.
[Reviewer-identified] The claimed approximately 99% optimality and near-perfect reconstruction have no numerical evidence in the PDF.
[Reviewer-identified] Appendix A is a selected qualitative gallery with no feature denominator, selection rule, rater protocol, or uncertainty.

[Reviewer-identified] The model description conflicts over dynamic encoder indicators versus a single static encoder pass, and omits enough architectural and training detail to prevent exact paper-only reproduction.
[Reviewer-identified] Qualitative tuning and qualitative evaluation on the same distribution create circular selection pressure.
[Reviewer-identified] The study has no negative control such as an untrained solver, random directions, earlier layers, or a reconstruction-matched nonsparse decomposition.
[Reviewer-identified] The claim to be the first activation-based interpretability study in operations research depends on an unstated literature-search boundary.
failure_modes: Sparse latents may encode coordinate or boundary statistics that are visually salient but unused by the decoder.
Overlaying ten instances and averaging activation can erase conditional structure or manufacture an apparently smooth geometric motif.
Human inspection may preferentially retain recognizable features and omit the majority that are polysemantic, unstable, dead, or unclear.
A reconstruction-optimal dictionary can rotate or split across training seeds, making named features non-identifiable.
Features learned on uniform N=100 instances can fail under clustered, ring, larger, smaller, or real road-network distributions.
The stated thresholded TopK equation can produce fewer active features and different magnitudes than the claimed retain-k operation.
Incomplete solver reporting can hide a weak or unstable policy whose representations do not generalize to competitive routing systems.
Final-layer residuals can mix many upstream computations, so a feature direction need not correspond to a localized circuit or heuristic.
reusable_insights: When importing SAE methods into combinatorial optimization, separate representation discovery from causal validation against action logits and objective value.
Predefine geometric feature scores and use a held-out instance set before selecting SAE hyperparameters or display examples.
Report solver quality and representation quality in the same artifact: instance count, gap distribution, seeds, reconstruction error, sparsity, dead features, and stability are minimum controls.

Use negative controls—random directions, untrained policies, coordinate-only baselines, alternative layers, and reconstruction-matched decompositions—to test whether visual motifs exceed generic geometry.
Test feature alignment under permutation, rotation, translation, scaling, size changes, and distribution shifts before assigning semantic names.
A visually intuitive node feature is only a mechanistic explanation after interventions predictably change decoder choices or tour length.
Equations implementing top-k sparsification should distinguish masking the largest k values from subtracting the kth-order statistic.
open_questions: What exact Concorde-relative gap distribution, sample count, runtime, and seed variance support the approximately 99% headline?
How many SAE features are dead, polysemantic, stable across seeds, and reproducibly classifiable under a blinded protocol?
Do the boundary and separator features causally alter decoder logits, selected edges, and final tour length under patching or ablation?
Are similar geometric patterns present in an untrained network, coordinate-only embedding, random projection, PCA, ICA, or dense autoencoder?
Do feature dictionaries align across solver seeds, SAE seeds, layers, architectures, and RL objectives?
Do claimed cluster-sensitive features persist and matter on explicitly clustered instances rather than uniform point clouds that happen to contain local density variation?
How do features transform under Euclidean symmetries and node permutations, and are purported concepts invariant or equivariant as expected?
Which implementation is intended by the dynamic encoder-feature description, and does resolving it change the learned representations?
Can a preregistered quantitative geometry benchmark predict which SAE configuration will also be causally faithful?

competitive_landscape.title: Attention, Learn to Solve Routing Problems!
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct neural-routing architecture and REINFORCE-training predecessor for attention-based construction policies.
competitive_landscape.difference: Kool et al. establish the attention-model solver and report quantitative routing comparisons; the target paper analyzes a related RL4CO policy with an SAE but omits a comparable solver-results table.

competitive_landscape.title: RL4CO: an Extensive Reinforcement Learning for Combinatorial Optimization Benchmark
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct framework and benchmarking source for the RL4CO solver family used by the target.
competitive_landscape.difference: RL4CO evaluates many environments, models, and baselines; the target uses the framework for one uniform N=100 interpretability case study without its breadth of quantitative controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Combinatorial Interpretability of Neural Computation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary mechanistic-interpretability work centered on combinatorial structure.
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies weight-centric exact structure in small Boolean computations, whereas the target performs activation-dictionary analysis on a larger TSP policy; the former offers a different evidentiary route from qualitative SAE overlays.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct top-k sparse-autoencoder methodological predecessor invoked by the target.
competitive_landscape.difference: Gao et al. develop top-k SAEs and quantitative evaluation/scaling methodology for language models; the target transfers the technique to TSP residuals but does not report comparable metrics, and miscites its arXiv identifier as 2306.04093.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning the Travelling Salesperson Problem Requires Rethinking Generalization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct evaluation and generalization critique for learned TSP solvers.
competitive_landscape.difference: Joshi et al. emphasize generalization controls and cross-distribution/size behavior; the target interprets only uniform N=100 representations and defers those controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Combinatorial Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Bello et al. establish RL-trained neural tour construction; the target's incremental contribution is post-hoc activation interpretation rather than a new solver objective or architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: NeuroLKH: Combining Deep Learning Model with Lin-Kernighan-Helsgaun Heuristic for Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct high-performance learned-plus-classical TSP alternative relevant to solver quality and hybridization.
competitive_landscape.difference: NeuroLKH couples learned guidance with an explicit classical search heuristic and quantitative TSP benchmarks; the target analyzes a pure construction policy and only proposes hybrid solver insight as future work.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first activation-based mechanistic-interpretability study in operations research and report human-aligned boundary, cluster, and separator directions in a competitive RL-trained TSP solver.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper does apply a top-k SAE to a final encoder residual stream and presents a TSP-specific qualitative feature gallery, but supplies no systematic priority search, causal test, quantitative feature evaluation, or complete routing benchmark.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is an early domain-transfer demonstration of SAE inspection for neural combinatorial optimization. The SAE, neural routing architecture, RL training, and concerns about TSP generalization are established by exact prior work; the paper does not yet support the stronger novelty of a validated mechanistic account of TSP reasoning.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text audit of the exact indexed 11-page arXiv:2510.21693v1 PDF, including pp. 1–8 main text, pp. 9–10 references, and p. 11 Appendix A; Figures 1–4 were visually inspected. The paper has no numbered result tables or proofs, and Appendix A contains only Figure 4. All 11 pages have usable extracted text. Exact indexed provenance: PDF SHA-256 4b846d4067f1fc01a28883c67bebdc8e3a92344cc2ce9b8d0d616efa27f73dbc; extracted-text SHA-256 47e5ecbbb39c090ba26e3313221ef6eba9b84baeaf2900bb1e08d05f9d549168. The official arXiv history was checked through 2026-08-23 and v1 is current. Competitor records were checked against the exact official revisions named in each version-pinned URL. Reference [10]'s 2306.04093 identifier is a paper error; the official SAE record is 2406.04093v1. Claims of approximately 99% optimality and near-perfect reconstruction are retained only as unsupported author reports, not independently verified outcomes.
